title: Decoding inherited genetics to cancer susceptibility
summary: A multi-institutional study in mice shows inherited genetic background shapes how tumors arise and evolve after DNA damage. By exposing genetically diverse mouse strains to the same liver carcinogen and sequencing nearly 600 tumours, researchers found common activation of the MAPK pathway but different driver mutations, pathway activities and whole-genome duplication tendencies across strains. Findings suggest inherited genetics and population diversity should inform screening, prevention and precision medicine, though human relevance requires further study.
content:
Scientists report direct experimental evidence that inherited genetic background strongly influences cancer susceptibility and tumour evolution.

In a study published in Nature, researchers from the University of Cambridge, the University of Edinburgh, Yale and other institutions used an experimental design that controlled environmental exposures to isolate the effect of inherited genetics. The team bred four mouse strains representing genetic diversity comparable to that seen in human populations and exposed all animals to the same single dose of the liver carcinogen diethylnitrosamine (DEN) at 15 days of age.

Because exposure, dose and age were identical for all animals, the researchers eliminated many environmental confounders that complicate human cohort studies. They then sequenced the genomes of almost 600 tumours, profiled gene activity and examined untreated mice to compare spontaneous tumour formation across strains. Using these data they reconstructed the evolutionary trajectories of individual tumours from their initiating mutations.

Across all strains, cancers nearly always acquired mutations that activated the same cancer-promoting signalling cascade, the MAPK pathway, which controls cell growth and differentiation and is implicated in many cancer types. Crucially, however, the particular driver mutations that emerged differed by genetic background and in turn altered activity of other cancer-associated signalling pathways.

The study also found striking variation in the frequency of whole-genome duplication — an event in which the entire chromosome set is doubled — depending on inherited genetics. Those differences indicate that genetic background not only affects which mutations arise but also shapes broader genomic changes and the downstream molecular circuitry of tumours.

Senior author Professor Duncan Odom, who led the work while at the CRUK Cambridge Institute and is now at DKFZ in Heidelberg, said: "Cancer does not arise entirely by chance. Although tumours often reach the same biological endpoint, the path to that endpoint is determined by an individual's genetic background." First author Dr Sarah Aitken added that the findings point to the need to consider inherited genetics and population diversity in future prevention and screening strategies.

The authors highlight implications for precision medicine: if inherited genetics influence both cancer risk and tumour evolutionary paths, responses to DNA-damaging treatments could vary by patient background. That supports tailoring diagnostics and therapies to genetic context rather than relying solely on tumour histology or exposure history.

Researchers caution that these experiments were carried out in mice and further work is required to determine how findings translate to humans. Nonetheless, the controlled experimental evidence addresses a long-standing challenge in human studies, where lifestyle, exposure and environmental variability mask inherited contributions to cancer susceptibility.

The project was a years-long international collaboration involving the University of Cambridge, University of Edinburgh, Yale and other centres in Europe and the US, and was largely carried out at the Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute. Funding came from Cancer Research UK, the Medical Research Council, the European Research Council and Wellcome.

The authors say the results provide a new lens on cancer origins and evolution: inherited genetic variation can influence mutation processes, driver selection, pathway activation and large-scale chromosomal events. If replicated and extended in human studies, this insight could reshape screening priorities, risk models and the development of personalised prevention and treatment strategies.

content.title: Decoding inherited genetics to cancer susceptibility
content.content:
Scientists have found the first direct evidence of the powerful role our genetic makeup plays in influencing our risk of cancer, with inherited genes interacting with acquired genetic mutations to shape how tumors evolve.The findings could explain why some people are more susceptible to cancer than others in the same environment and suggest that future cancer prevention and screening strategies may need to account more carefully for inherited genetics and population diversity.The research, published today in Nature and carried out in mice, suggests that responses to DNA-damaging cancer treatments could differ depending on a patient’s background genetics, strengthening the case for a more personalised approach to treatment.Tumors arise when our DNA accumulates errors, or mutations, causing the cells to grow faster and ignore signals that would otherwise instruct damaged cells to die before they can cause harm. Environmental exposures – for example, cigarette smoke or sunlight – influence how much DNA damage occurs, and inherited genetic alterations can alter how many mutations accumulate.Not everyone exposed to the same environmental risk factors will develop cancer, however. Most smokers do not develop lung cancer – and some non-smokers develop lung cancer. The reason why is almost certainly related to our inherited genetic makeup, but finding direct evidence has proved challenging in patient cohort studies. Even though many studies have suggested that inherited genetic differences affect cancer risk, proving this link has been difficult because individuals within – and between – human populations vary in lifestyle, environment, and exposure history.The study is the result of years of international collaboration, between the University of Cambridge, University of Edinburgh, and others around Europe and the US, and was co-led by Professor Duncan Odom, Dr Sarah Aitken and Professor Martin Taylor.In experiments largely carried out at the Cancer Research UK (CRUK) Cambridge Institute at the University of Cambridge, scientists developed an experimental approach that allowed them to control environmental factors experimentally and show that genetic background itself can alter how tumors arise and evolve.The team bred four strains of mice with varying susceptibility to liver cancer, spanning a level of genetic diversity comparable to that seen in human populations. They then exposed the mice to a single dose of the liver carcinogen diethylnitrosamine (DEN). DEN is found in tobacco smoke and some processed foods and is known to cause DNA damage in liver cells, leading to mutations that can initiate tumor growth.Because every mouse received the same dose at the same age – 15 days of age – under controlled conditions, the researchers were able to eliminate the environmental variation that confounds studies in humans.They then sequenced the genomes of almost 600 tumors and analysed the gene activity that developed as well as examining the untreated mice to compare spontaneous tumor formation across strains. Using this data, they were able to reconstruct how each tumor evolved from its original cancer-causing mutation.Across all mouse strains, cancers nearly always acquired a cancer-driving mutation that activated the same cancer-promoting signalling system, called the MAPK pathway. This is a multi-step cascade of molecular signals that controls important life processes, including cell growth and cell differentiation, and plays a key role in numerous types of cancer.However, depending on the inherited genetics of the mouse, the particular driver mutation that was acquired altered the activity of other cancer-associated signalling pathways, as well as causing a striking tendency for whole-genome duplication, an event in which the entire set of chromosomes is doubled.Senior author Professor Duncan Odom, who led the research while at the CRUK Cambridge Institute and is now based at DKFZ (German Cancer Research Centre) in Heidelberg, Germany, said: “Cancer does not arise entirely by chance. Although tumors often reach the same biological endpoint, the path to that endpoint is determined by an individual’s genetic background.“We’ve been able to show for the first time the extent to which genetic background influences both the mutation processes and the pathways leading to tumor development.”The researchers say the findings have implications for cancer screening and precision medicine.First author Dr/ Sarah Aitken, Assistant Professor at Yale School of Medicine, who also worked on the research at the CRUK Cambridge Institute, said: “If genetic background influences both cancer risk and the evolutionary trajectory of tumors, future cancer prevention and screening strategies will need to take into account inherited genetics and population diversity.“Similarly, how people respond to cancer drugs is likely to differ depending on their inherited genetics, and so we may need to tailor our diagnostics and treatments accordingly.”This study gives us a fascinating hint that our inherited genes might have a big influence on the way that cancers develop after DNA damage.“We still need to see more research before we can understand what this means in humans, but this finding could change our understanding of how cancer starts, and lead to more powerful and precise ways of tackling cancer, “Dr Sam Godfrey, research information lead, Cancer Research UK.The research was largely funded by Cancer Research UK, the Medical Research Council, European Research Council and Wellcome.University of Cambridge

content.title: Decoding inherited genetics to cancer susceptibility
content.author: aditya_gupta

markdown_content:
Scientists report direct experimental evidence that inherited genetic background strongly influences cancer susceptibility and tumour evolution.

## Study overview
In a study published in Nature, researchers from the University of Cambridge, the University of Edinburgh, Yale and other institutions used an experimental design that controlled environmental exposures to isolate the effect of inherited genetics.

## Experimental design
- The team bred four mouse strains representing genetic diversity comparable to that seen in human populations.
- All animals were exposed to the same single dose of the liver carcinogen diethylnitrosamine (DEN) at 15 days of age.
- Because exposure, dose and age were identical for all animals, the researchers eliminated many environmental confounders that complicate human cohort studies.
- They sequenced the genomes of almost 600 tumours, profiled gene activity and examined untreated mice to compare spontaneous tumour formation across strains.
- Using these data they reconstructed the evolutionary trajectories of individual tumours from their initiating mutations.

## Key findings
- Across all strains, cancers nearly always acquired mutations that activated the same cancer-promoting signalling cascade, the MAPK pathway, which controls cell growth and differentiation and is implicated in many cancer types.
- Crucially, the particular driver mutations that emerged differed by genetic background and in turn altered activity of other cancer-associated signalling pathways.
- The study found striking variation in the frequency of whole-genome duplication — an event in which the entire chromosome set is doubled — depending on inherited genetics.
- Those differences indicate that genetic background not only affects which mutations arise but also shapes broader genomic changes and the downstream molecular circuitry of tumours.

## Author perspectives
> “Cancer does not arise entirely by chance. Although tumours often reach the same biological endpoint, the path to that endpoint is determined by an individual's genetic background.”  
— Professor Duncan Odom, senior author

> “The findings point to the need to consider inherited genetics and population diversity in future prevention and screening strategies.”  
— Dr Sarah Aitken, first author

## Implications for precision medicine
- If inherited genetics influence both cancer risk and tumour evolutionary paths, responses to DNA-damaging treatments could vary by patient background.
- This supports tailoring diagnostics and therapies to genetic context rather than relying solely on tumour histology or exposure history.

## Limitations
The researchers caution that these experiments were carried out in mice and further work is required to determine how findings translate to humans. Nonetheless, the controlled experimental evidence addresses a long-standing challenge in human studies, where lifestyle, exposure and environmental variability mask inherited contributions to cancer susceptibility.

## Collaboration and funding
The project was a years-long international collaboration involving the University of Cambridge, University of Edinburgh, Yale and other centres in Europe and the US, and was largely carried out at the Cancer Research UK Cambridge Institute. Funding came from Cancer Research UK, the Medical Research Council, the European Research Council and Wellcome.

## Conclusion
The authors say the results provide a new lens on cancer origins and evolution: inherited genetic variation can influence mutation processes, driver selection, pathway activation and large-scale chromosomal events. If replicated and extended in human studies, this insight could reshape screening priorities, risk models and the development of personalised prevention and treatment strategies.
